timeline.eyebrow: 07 / A TIME MACHINE WITH NO STEAM REQUIRED
timeline.title: Ada's time machine.
timeline.description: Six stops through the life and legacy of Ada Lovelace. Historical facts with sources and clearly labelled fictional comments.
timeline.intro: Choose a year. History has a source. Our Ada has an opinion.
timeline.comment: What might Ada say about this today?
timeline.disclaimer: We invented the following comments. They are not authentic quotations from Ada Lovelace.
timeline.imageNote: The historical portrait illustrates the person, not the specific event or its year.
timeline.chalon: Watercolour portrait from around 1840, attributed to A. E. Chalon. Public domain.
timeline.carpenter: Margaret Sarah Carpenter, portrait of Ada Lovelace, 1836. Public domain.
timeline.claudet: Antoine Claudet, daguerreotype of Ada Lovelace, dated 1843 or 1850 in the source. Public domain.
timeline.altChalon: Watercolour portrait of Ada Lovelace in a light dress with dark lace.
timeline.altCarpenter: Painted portrait of Ada Lovelace in a white dress with a red sash.
timeline.altClaudet: Historical photograph of Ada Lovelace in an oval gold frame.
timeline.1815.title: Hello, Ada.
timeline.1815.fact: Augusta Ada Byron, later known as Ada Lovelace, was born in 1815. Her parents were Annabella Milbanke and the poet Lord Byron.
timeline.1815.joke: I brought a new kind of poetry into the family. No syntax yet, but exceptionally loud error notifications.
timeline.1833.title: The meeting that changed the brief.
timeline.1833.fact: Seventeen-year-old Ada met Charles Babbage and saw a demonstration of part of his calculating machine. This began a connection that later developed into a collaboration.
timeline.1833.joke: I went to a party. I left with a long-term project and absolutely no estimate for hardware delivery.
timeline.1840.title: Mathematics by post.
timeline.1840.fact: In 1840 and 1841, Ada studied advanced mathematics through correspondence with Augustus De Morgan. Their surviving letters document her learning and her questions.
timeline.1840.joke: My online course had a latency of several days. Still, nobody ever said: can you hear me?
timeline.1843.title: Notes that outgrew the margins.
timeline.1843.fact: Her English translation of Menabrea's article on the Analytical Engine was published with extensive notes. Note G contains a procedure for calculating Bernoulli numbers.
timeline.1843.joke: I only added a few comments. The reviewer ordered another teapot as a precaution.
timeline.1852.title: A life ends. A legacy continues.
timeline.1852.fact: Ada Lovelace died in 1852. Her published notes remained part of computing history and later discussions about what computers could do.
timeline.1852.joke: A message for future teams: write documentation that can outlive the project's original author.
timeline.1983.title: Her name gets a compiler.
timeline.1983.fact: The first standard for the Ada programming language was published in 1983. The language honours her legacy with its name; she neither created nor used it herself.
timeline.1983.joke: At last, they named something after me. I do hope the error messages have good manners.
workshop.title: Program a punched card.
workshop.description: An interactive workshop: build a program from cards, reorder the steps and watch a calculation or a cup of tea take shape.
workshop.intro: Choose a task, add cards and start the machine. The butler will do exactly what you tell him. Even when it makes no sense.
workshop.disclaimer: A modern educational game inspired by punched cards. It is not a reconstruction of Babbage's machine or Ada's historical program.
workshop.mathGoal: Goal: get the number 10 into memory and display it with the final card.
workshop.teaGoal: Goal: water, heat, tea leaves, brewing and serving. The order is part of the recipe.
workshop.limit: Up to 12 cards. Use the up and down buttons to reorder them. Everything works with a keyboard too.
workshop.empty: Nothing here yet. The butler is enjoying the peace. Add your first card.
workshop.ready: The machine is waiting for a program.
workshop.edited: Program updated. Execution will start from the beginning.
workshop.paused: Program paused. You can continue or run one step.
workshop.full: Twelve cards will do. Remove one before adding another.
workshop.needCards: Add at least one card first.
workshop.didWater: Water is in the kettle. No hardware leaks so far.
workshop.didHeat: The water is at 95 °C. Simulated steam is free.
workshop.didLeaves: The leaves are in the water. Tea dependency loaded.
workshop.didSteep: The simulated tea has brewed. No actual three-minute wait required.
workshop.successMath: The result is 10. The program works. The butler requests a performance bonus.
workshop.successTea: Tea is ready. The algorithm is correct and the salon is hydrated.
workshop.errorPrefix: Program stopped. The butler cannot follow these instructions.
workshop.errorEmpty: The kettle is empty. Add water first.
workshop.errorCold: The water is not hot yet. Heat it first.
workshop.errorLeaves: Without leaves, it is just hot water. Add tea.
workshop.errorSteep: The tea needs to brew before you serve it.
workshop.errorRepeat: This step has already run. One cup of tea does not need two initialisations.
workshop.errorGoal: You displayed {0}, but the goal is 10. Check the order and values.
workshop.errorOutput: The final card is missing: display the result or serve the tea.
workshop.errorLast: The output card must be last. Move it to the end.
workshop.errorOverflow: That number is too large for this little workshop. Try a shorter program.
workshop.errorUnknown: This card does not belong to the selected task.
advice.title: Ask the countess.
advice.description: Ada's fictional programming advice: bugs, AI, deadlines, meetings and learning to code, with Victorian humour.
advice.intro: Six modern problems. One suspiciously well-prepared lady from the 19th century.
advice.disclaimer: Original humorous dialogues, not historical quotations. Answers are written in advance; this is not a live AI conversation.
advice.bug.q: Why does my code not work?
advice.bug.a: Dear visitor, my program had to wait for hardware too. Before blaming the universe, check the last line. And the one before it. The universe can wait.
advice.bug.tip: Reproduce the bug with the smallest possible example. Compare the expected and actual results, then fix one thing at a time.
advice.ai.a: It may write you a loop. Someone still needs to work out why you wanted to repeat the same mistake a thousand times.
advice.ai.tip: Use AI as an assistant. Learn to understand the task, read the resulting code and check how it behaves.
advice.deadline.q: What if I cannot meet the deadline?
advice.deadline.a: Say so before the client starts using yesterday as a delivery date. The Analytical Engine had a complicated schedule too.
advice.deadline.tip: Explain what is finished, what is blocking progress and the realistic next step. Agree on a smaller scope or a new deadline.
advice.meeting.a: If its only outcome is let's arrange another meeting, I suggest correspondence. It is slower, but at least nobody shares the wrong window.
advice.meeting.tip: Ask for the meeting's purpose and the decision needed. A simple project update can often be sent in writing.
advice.learn.q: How do I learn to program?
advice.learn.a: Start with a small problem that interests you. I chose a machine that did not exist yet. You need not copy that part of my approach.
advice.learn.tip: Build a small project, break it into steps and check the result after each change. Ask why the solution works.
advice.deploy.q: Can I deploy a change on Friday evening?
advice.deploy.a: Certainly. One can also pour evening tea into a keyboard. Being technically possible does not make something a good plan.
advice.deploy.tip: Before deploying, check the change, prepare a way back to a working version and agree on who will be available if something goes wrong.
news.eyebrow: 10 / A NEWSROOM POWERED BY STEAM AND SATIRE
news.title: The Salon Tech Gazette.
news.description: A fictional Victorian technology newspaper: a steam cloud, meetings by letter and very serious tea troubles.
news.intro: The 1843-ish edition. Every story is invented. The editorial outrage is a performance.
news.motto: Everything that never happened, all in one place.
news.ad: AN ADVERTISEMENT WE ALSO MADE UP
news.adText: TeaScript Premium: the same tea, now with an invoice. First sip included in the trial.
news.steam.title: Steam Cloud escapes up the chimney again.
news.steam.summary: Customers report data showers. The operator recommends a bucket and a local backup.
news.steam.body: The fictional company Steam Cloud announced today that its infrastructure has moved into the upper atmosphere. The migration was unplanned and caused by a draught. File recovery will resume after the rain. The editors note that ordinary paper may not scale, but it rarely leaves the room through the chimney.
news.hardware.title: Hardware arriving soon, says announcement from 1843.
news.hardware.summary: The project plan has three phases: design, waiting and renaming waiting as research.
news.hardware.body: Our fictional supplier has unveiled a new order status: almost probably on its way. Meanwhile, programmers are testing on paper, which boasts excellent battery life. This is satire about modern projects, not a real statement by Charles Babbage or a historical news report.
news.meeting.title: Programmer declines meeting that could have been a letter.
news.meeting.summary: A request for a clear meeting agenda shakes the salon. A working group has been formed.
news.meeting.body: A fictional committee met for two hours to decide whether to meet again tomorrow. The Ada of our alternative reality sent a single paragraph with the solution. The committee praised her initiative and proposed an hour-long presentation of the paragraph. Meanwhile, the butler solved the problem by stopping the tea refills.
news.bug.title: Bug in machine demands recognition as a feature.
news.bug.summary: It has six legs, no documentation and very strong views on backwards compatibility.
news.bug.body: In our fictional salon, a beetle refuses to move out until it gets its own ticket. It claims that unpredictable results encourage creativity. The editors suggest a safe relocation to the garden and a fix for the program. This story is not a historical account of the origin of the term bug.
news.biscuit.title: Research: one biscuit improves reviewer's mood.
news.biscuit.summary: The study has one participant. He insists on an immediate repeat of the experiment.
news.biscuit.body: In an entirely fictional experiment, an editor received a biscuit and stopped complaining about semicolons. The researchers draw no scientific conclusions, because the researchers do not exist either. The only reliable finding: the biscuits ran out before the code review comments did.
news.ai.title: TeaGPT promises a revolution. So far, it predicts the next sip.
news.ai.summary: The fictional model was trained on three tea leaves and one piece of society gossip.
news.ai.body: The fictional service TeaGPT answers every question with it depends on the water temperature. Investors in our imaginary salon are delighted, because the answer works even when asked about the business model. The editors recommend checking claims and drinking ordinary tea without a subscription.
